opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing I'd prioritize is data, and specifically the infrastructure for collecting it at scale. In robotics, unlike language or vision, there's no internet's worth of robot interaction data just lying around. So whoever figures out how to gather lots of diverse, high-quality data efficiently, whether through teleoperation, deployment, or some clever mix, has a real advantage.

Closely tied to that, I'd bet on generality over narrow solutions. A lot of past robotics companies built a bespoke system for one task in one environment, and it was brittle and expensive to adapt. What we've seen recently is that training a single model on data from many tasks, environments, and even different robot bodies often generalizes better than a specialist. So I'd want the whole technical stack designed around that, so every new task makes the system better overall instead of being a one-off engineering project.

I'd also be careful about hardware. It's tempting to build your own robot from scratch, but that can eat years and a lot of money. I'd use hardware that's good enough, reasonably cheap, and robust, and put the differentiation in the learning and the data. If the models are good, they can make up for a lot of imperfection in the hardware.

Finally, I'd think hard about deployment and the path to real value. You don't need to solve general-purpose robotics on day one, but you want early use cases where robots can do something useful and also generate data that feeds back into the model. Getting that flywheel going, where deployment produces data, data improves the model, and a better model unlocks more deployment, is what I'd be aiming for from the start.

r001.rationale: It recommends finding early useful deployment opportunities and explains that deployment generates data that improves the model, creating a feedback loop for learning.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing I'd prioritize is data, and being really thoughtful about where it comes from. In language, the internet handed everyone a massive dataset for free. Robotics doesn't have that. So the central question for any robotics company right now is: what's your data engine? How are you going to collect diverse, high-quality data on real robots, in real environments, at a scale that actually lets the model generalize? That's not a side problem, that is the company.

The second thing, which is closely related, is getting robots out into the world early. There's a temptation to stay in the lab until things are polished, but the lab is a terrible proxy for the messiness of real homes and real workplaces. Every deployment teaches you something about the distribution you actually need to cover, and it also generates data. So I'd want a product wedge that lets us deploy quickly, even if the capability is narrow at first, and then expand from there.

Third, I'd think hard about the hardware-software interplay. I'm a learning person, so I believe most of the intelligence should come from the model rather than from clever engineering of the mechanical system. But the hardware still needs to be reliable and cheap enough that you can have a lot of robots running for a long time. If your platform breaks every few hours, you can't collect data, and you can't learn. So I'd prioritize robustness and cost over peak performance.

And finally, the team. Robotics is unusual because you need people who are excellent at machine learning and people who are excellent at building physical systems, and historically those communities haven't talked to each other much. Getting both in the same room, with a shared belief that scaling learning on real-world data is the path, that's probably the thing that determines whether everything else works.

r001.rationale: It recommends getting robots into the world early, explaining that each deployment teaches the company about real-world conditions and generates data.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by finding a task that’s useful to someone and that a robot can realistically do well today. There’s a temptation to start with a general-purpose robot and then figure out the application. I’d want a specific application where you can get robots deployed, learn from the failures, and make the system better.

And I’d think about the data collection process from day one. When the robot gets stuck, can a person help it? Can you capture that intervention and use it to improve the policy? The deployment should give you both a useful product and a way to keep learning.

So I’d prioritize the task, the reliability of the full system, and that learning loop. You can have a really impressive model, but if the robot needs someone standing next to it all day, the economics are going to be difficult.

r001.rationale: The response recommends getting robots deployed so the company can learn from failures and improve the system.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by finding a task where the robot can provide value even if it can’t do everything. There’s a temptation to start with a general-purpose robot, but then you’re trying to solve the hardware, the learning, and the business all at once. I’d want a fairly narrow initial application, with a path to expanding what the robot can do.

And I’d prioritize the data collection loop from day one. When the robot fails, can you capture that failure, get useful supervision, and actually improve the system? Can you do that across a fleet without requiring an engineer to babysit every robot? I think that infrastructure is going to matter a lot.

So I’d choose the task and the hardware together, with an eye toward getting robots into use early. You want deployment to help you learn what to build next, and you want the data from that deployment to make the product better.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends getting robots into use early and says deployment will help the company learn what to build next.
